utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the accused resumes cross-examination, may I explain something to the Chamber in private session for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you gave the following explanation: Since you had not been in your village for 17 years, you could not remember more people. We established yesterday that you remembered only four names; is that right? Because you had not been in your village for many years, and that was the explanation why you could not remember more names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which names you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't matter which names. My question was how come you could not remember any more names, only these four names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I did not recognise any more people than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not recognise them because you hadn't lived there for 17 years; is that right? And was that the explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That explanation is rather flimsy in view of the first thing that was shown here yesterday. I'm not going to mention your village. I'm not going to refer to it specifically, but we do have here your details, and we looked at them or, rather, you looked at them when we started, that is, 023 -- 0293543. It's tab 1, actually. That's easier. Tab 1. That's where your details are. And then you say under point 2, from 1975 until mid-1990, during the week I lived in Belgrade and during the weekend, and then you give the name of your village. So during all those years, you went to your village, and it was only during workdays that you went to work in Belgrade. How do you explain this then? How do you explain what you said, that you hadn't been in the village for 17 years and that's why you didn't know people when you were there every week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be at home. I would work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so you didn't have contact with other villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The population of that village is a couple of hundred people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I know the people who live in my village, but they are not the ones who took part in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I asked you and you said that you did not mention this at all but you did manage to recognise the Serbs, the guards, soldiers, whichever way you want to call them. And then you asked me where it said so that you knew them, and I'm going to read this to you now where it says so. Of course I have the English version, in all fairness of that statement. That is page 5. And the number is 00453878. In the last paragraph it says: "[In English] Throughout our detention in the hangar, we noticed the guards worked in three shifts of eight hours each. Each shift had eight guards and out of the total number of the guards, I recognised three. They were Ratko Spasojevic from the village of Setici, Vlajko Jovanovic from the village of Petkovci, and Mujo [sic] (LNU)," [Interpretation] I don't know what that means, "[In English] from Trsic or Celopek and everybody called Mujo as Captain." So that's what you wrote here, that you knew these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that man. It isn't "Mujo," it's "Mijo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, "Mijo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the men from Trsic who were detained addressed him by his name. They knew his name was Mijo, and the rest called him Captain. As for Vlajko, I saw him once when he came and when he said, "How come there is so much vermin around here? If somebody wants to kill himself I will help them immediately." And then she left. As for Ratko Spasojevic, I did not see him at all. I had seen him only in town before. So that's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here at the end there's a sentence that reads as follows, because you say you saw this man once and he said how come there is so much vermin around here and then you never saw this other man that's what you say. "[In English] I knew Ratko and Vlajko very well because we had played football together as youngsters." [Interpretation] So you knew them well. It's not that you saw him once. You said that you knew them well. And now you say that you saw one of them only once and the other one you say that you never saw. What is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truth is that I know both of them but I did not see Ratko. I saw Vlajko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean you saw Ratko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that Muradif saw him. That's what it says here. That's what it should say there. This is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "[In English] I recognised three." [Interpretation] "I recognised three, that's what it says. Ratko Spasojevic from Setici, Vlajko Jovanovic from Petkovci, and Mijo from Trsic or Celopek." So that is what is written here. Please tell me, Mr. 1098, what is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truth is what I said only awhile ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how come this is written here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how come, but obviously they didn't understand me properly. I don't know English, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber would like copies of the statement without prejudice as to whether it is ultimately to be produced as an exhibit to follow this sort of text or argument by the accused, because I think the text really needs to be seen for the witness to be able to respond fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see a copy. Which was the passage again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 5 at the foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that all of this was mistranslated, that you recognised them, that you knew their names and then you explained that you had played football together as youngsters with these two. So all of this is due to mistranslation. Is that your assertion, Mr. 1098?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Ratko Spasojevic and Vlajko, it is true that I used to play football with them. And Ratko Spasojevic was born the same year I was. But it is also true this is what is written here. And I gave the correction because of what the translator said then. I said that it was not written properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what you said and then you denied it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not deny it. The interpreter did not understand me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the interpreter invented Ratko Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the interpreter did not invent Ratko Spasojevic. I said that Muradif had seen Ratko Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remember, both of you, allow the other one to finish asking the question and that includes you, Mr. Milosevic, but Witness B-1098, would you watch the accused's microphone and make sure it's off before you answer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this correction, yet again you have this statement 0304841 -- 8141, and you correct what it says here, and you say: "I mentioned that Ratko Spasojevic was a guard." And then you say: "I did not see Ratko Spasojevic personally. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That is the kind of statement I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's the correction you made. So you heard from your nephew Muradif that he was one of the guards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muradif.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you correct yourself and you say that you never saw him come and take prisoners out of room 1 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but the question has given a full name in a few lines back of the nephew. I was careful not to use full names. Can the passage be redacted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it may be safer to go into private session for these questions. While you're asking questions about these people, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I'm not going to put any more questions, but no doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you come to any occasion you're going to ask questions about individuals, we'll go into private certification but we'll stay in open session for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what kind of uniforms were these men that you mentioned wearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say -- I mean, since you mentioned the men you knew from your village, the men you knew were there, do you consider them to be the JNA or these reservists from your village, what do you consider them to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not consider them to be the JNA, but I do consider them to be the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they're not from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're from the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 5, in paragraph 6, you say that you know this Mijo, nicknamed Captain, and you don't know his last name, and you don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session now. You've been told if we were mentioning the names we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going into private session, and we're going to stay there. Yes. We'll stop all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1098, on page 7 of your statement you claim that during this alleged execution that you describe in that small room, 3 by 3, you were shot at from two machine-guns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two of the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two guards with two machine-guns shot at you in this small room 3 by 3 and you say that there were 20 of you in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said around 20. And now whether both were shooting in that room 3 by 3, I mean, if I were to shut people into a room 3 by 3 and if I were to start shooting, I wonder whether anybody's going to notice who was actually doing the shooting, both people or just one man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is in line 1. You say 20 detainees. That's what you say. So as they were shooting from two machine-guns at close range in a closed area, they allegedly carried out an execution, and you're the only one who was not hit. They managed to kill the rest, the 19 remaining people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't say two machine-guns here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you can't see it, I'm going to tell you where it is. You say -- this is the first paragraph, if you disregard the paragraph that started on the previous page. "There were two guards who were wearing SMB uniforms and were armed with machine-guns." And then you say: "As soon as we had our backs towards the guards, they started to shoot at us with their machine-guns."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why do you say I don't see machine-guns in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I meant. I didn't mean this paragraph, the one that you just referred to now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. All right. Is it correct that on that occasion although you were not hit you passed out? You say out of fear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still don't know until the present day what it was really like, whether I had passed out or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the last sentence in this paragraph. "I was not hit by the bullets but probably out of fright I fell unconscious." That is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put it quite properly, that most probably I passed out during the shooting, and I fell. And when I came to, which means that I did pass out, then I heard moaning, screams, cries, and what not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were unconscious? How can you then claim on page 7 in paragraph 3 that the guards, afterwards, shot from two machine-guns, and you claim that they killed 19 men? They did not hit you. You were not even wounded. And then they immediately entered the next room and then they shot detainees there, and you were unconscious in the meantime. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was only this period of crisis. Perhaps it was only a minute or -- a second or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were unconscious for only a second or two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a very interesting explanation. A man passes out and then I knows that he was unconscious only for a second or two and then he hears everything else. Very interesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Milosevic, that this didn't happen, that the witness wasn't there and didn't hear and see these things? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm suggesting, Mr. May, is this witness is not telling the truth at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you're saying it either, telling it either. I'm not a politician. All I'm doing is telling the truth and the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 1098, you're talking here. I'm not doing the talking. On page 7, paragraph 4, you say that you heard a truck starting, and you peeped outside the room to see whether they had left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you weren't unconscious then already at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Give me the names of those 19 people. Which of those 19 people who were with you do you know by name, of the ones who were killed, of those 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know four, four of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know those four men, and they were altogether with you over there in that group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that, "I was too scared to inspect the crime scene." That seems to be the language and terminology you use. "But I know that all those who were brought there with me were killed because they have never been seen since." That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's not only that those have never been seen since. Seven hundred of those people have never been seen since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is very specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how can you say that they have never been seen since when you don't know who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean I don't know who they were? I know who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you know four of them, which means that you don't know who the other 15 were. So how can you say they were never seen again when you don't know who they actually were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Milosevic, their families know very well who they were, the families that remained alive behind them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is being provoked by these kind of questions and the way they're being put. Now, Mr. B-1098, I realise you're being provoked by this sort of questioning, but don't get angry, please, and don't address him by his name. You're giving evidence to the Court, so address us and not him. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We seem to have cleared that up. So you claim that they have never been seen again although you don't know who they were. So you don't know that the people, who you don't know who they were, were never seen again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you claim that you were in a panic and jumped over a concrete fence of some kind, ran towards the Drina River which was about 2 to 300 metres from the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there is exactly 2 to 300 metres. It might have been 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Maybe 500.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't measure the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, tell me this then, please, how long did the drive in the truck last from Pilici up to the house that you were taken to, the so-called house that was called Gero's slaughterhouse where the executions took place? How long did you drive in the truck for? How long did that take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is that we were escorted by police car. Now, how long it lasted, none of us had watches, all of them were confiscated, so we weren't able to look at the time and see exactly how long, but you know how many kilometres it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give me a rough estimate. How long were you driven in the truck for? I don't want you to use a stopwatch to measure the time. Roughly, a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It could have lasted half an hour, 45 minutes. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you hidden in this place where you took refuge by the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in hiding -- I was in hiding by the Drina River from about 10:00 in the morning until dark fell. It was June, so that would make it around 9:00 in the evening. That's when it gets dark. So from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you're quoting a figure, the number of people, and you say a total of 193 people. You were within a distance of 500 metres and between you and them was this concrete fence which you say you jumped over. And then you go on to say in that same paragraph, in the previous sentence, that because of the concrete fence you weren't able to see the men getting out of the truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was 500 metres away from that place, and I said that I was roughly 500 metres away and heard the truck arrive and heard a repeated burst of gunfire. Then I heard the truck leave, and I heard it come back the way it came the previous time, bringing the first load or first lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said that very nicely, and you said that, "Because of the concrete fence, I wasn't able to see the people." That's what you say on page 7 now, tell me this, please. How is it possible for you not to be able to see the people but nevertheless you were able to count them from this distance of 500 metres where you were? How come you were able to count the people which you say you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He did not say he counted them. He made an estimate about the number of people on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on page 7, paragraph 6, you claim that besides yourself, another man, and I'm not going to name names here, survived because I assume we would have to go back into private session. But I'm sure you know who I'm talking about because you can look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am bearing that in mind, and I do know who the man is whom you mean. But he survived in that third tour, in that third lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, neither he nor anybody else is able to bear out your assertions and allegations. Am I right in saying that? Can somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't say what anybody else may know or not. Now, he's giving his evidence and he can tell you what he knows, but he can't say what other people know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. But what happened to that man? Tell us that. He survived, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer that, Your Honours? That man did survive, and he reached free territory and was killed during the war later on, subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was killed later on during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain this to me please now. You say, and I don't want to read the man's name out, that you learnt this fact later from some soldiers in Zaseok so witness at that time you didn't know of the man's existence and yet you claim that he was brought in for execution in that third group of people. So how could you say that at all? How can you claim that in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can claim that because there is a statement by him the same year he escaped just as I gave my statement the first year I escaped in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not testifying to that. You say that a statement by him exists, is that it? Fine. Now, then you go on to say on page 7, paragraph 7, that the next day you tried to go to your own village but you got lost, and then due to circumstance, you had to go back to the house where the execution was conducted. Is that what you say? Near the house where the execution took place, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we hear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to find -- if you were not able to find the path to your own village, how were you able to reach this particular house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wandered around where all that was going on. I was wandering around during the night in the rain. I'd like to ask anybody whether they'd be able to find their way at night in a downpour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1098, further down that page once again in paragraph 7, page 7, as you were there for the second time in that particular spot when it got dark you say that you started walking towards your village, and a name is mentioned there. I don't want to mention the name of the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I explained a moment ago that I was walking around at night and that I lost my way. And the day I spent hiding in the meadow, in the high grass, I stayed there the whole day hiding then came out when it was dark and found myself in that spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what happened later on once you had seen the bulldozers and all the rest that you described having seen. You described it at length. Afterwards, when it got dark, you say that you tried to go to your village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what the witness has said. Now, your time is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. really up. What is the question? You can ask one more after this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have several more questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time is up, so you can ask this question and then one more. It's difficult to see what the question is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, explain to me, because you were not able to find the way to your village during daylight, how were you able to find it at night, in the dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After those two nights spending -- spent wandering around Karakaj and once I had passed Celopek on that second night, I started climbing the mountain. I spent the night in the forests, and the next day I started out at daylight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question. May I ask it, please, Mr. May? I have several but please allow me enough time to ask one. I think it's essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twice during your oral testimony here yesterday in this courtroom you mentioned some women. On one occasion you said that women were crying out, the locals, the local women, along the roadside, and they shouted out to the men there, "Kill the balijas." And then on another occasion you say that one woman was shouting out through an aperture in the cinema hall. She said that if her brother was killed, she'd kill all of you. So tell me this now, please: Was that the reaction on the part of the women and the general atmosphere that prevailed after the crimes that the Muslim forces perpetrated against the Serb civilians in that region and then you were captured in those operations? Is that how it came about? How can you explain this reaction on the part of the women that they shouted out, "Kill the balijas," and the women who said if her brother was killed she would kill you. Who would kill her brother? What was going on that somebody was going to kill her brother?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer it. May I? When we arrived in Karakaj, there was -- there were a lot of women there, and they were all shouting, "Kill the balijas." Now, the woman who was looking out of the window, that woman was from Pilica. So these are different places; different villages. And she said that if her brother were to be killed, she would kill us. Now, I don't know, and may I ask a question, may I be allowed to ask a question, what were those people looking for in Kovacevici and Vitinci [phoen] when that is a purely Muslim settlement? Whereas they went to expel them and we were loyal citizens, Milosevic, down there. I wasn't captured during a battle or during any fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to start off by asking the witness to explain to the Trial Chamber several points linked to Exhibit 456, tab 4. I can't see the witness at all behind the screen. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday in response to a question from Mr. Nice, you explained this document, so I don't want to go back to those questions. You have the document before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, did you see the document for the first time in the Office of the Prosecutor, the OTP, or did you know about it later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice that the title on the document is as follows: It says review of transport of refugees as ordered by the interim government of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik and the Territorial Defence Staff of Zvornik. No mention is made of the JNA. It says here that everything was compiled on orders from the interim government of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. Did you happen to note that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that how it really was, that everything was organised by the Zvornik municipality, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at all events, you don't know that it was organised by the JNA, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who organised it. All I can -- all I do know is what I was able to read in the document, that -- the passages that follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I should like for a moment to go back to your statement, the one that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 24th of November, 1996, and I'd just like to focus on one particular paragraph which you explained to us yesterday. Let me just remind you of it. You said that most of the soldiers who had surrounded your village, and I'm not going to mention the name of your village, wore JNA uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were all kinds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And you said that you personally saw on that particular day, on the 1st of June, two tanks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say quite clearly, "I think that the soldiers in the olive-green uniforms were members of the regular forces of the JNA, whereas the soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms were locals, Chetniks"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I put it that way, but I said something similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what is says in the statement, but never mind. That was the statement you gave on the 24th of November, 1996, to the investigators of the Tribunal. Now, along with that statement I received from the OTP, from the Prosecution, Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 66, your own statement of the 17th of June, 1992, to the security centre of Tuzla, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the sector of the state security department. Do you remember that on the 17th of June, 1992, you did in fact give a statement to this body?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the statement translated by the OTP in English, and the number of it is the Serbian version, 0024672 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Copies are available as I indicated yesterday and coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that statement in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't need this. I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wish to remind you. Look at the beginning of that statement. You said the following: "As far as I can remember, about a month ago the village of Kula was attacked by the Chetniks." I won't read out the name of your village. And then the volunteers from your village, the 37 of them, went to defend Kula, that is, 37 volunteered and another five from another village. And since you didn't succeed in your defence, they returned home. Is that right correct, that from your village and other villages armed volunteers went to defend Kula one month before the 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that they went there. I don't know exactly whether there were 37 of them, but they did go to defend Kula. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But tell me this now. I read your statement very carefully, this particular statement. I don't have time to go into the details. There are many things that you have already said here. But you mostly said that all this was done by Chetniks. You even recognised a young man. And then in ten or so places you keep referring to the word "Chetniks," which means locals according to the statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP. Now, explain to me, please, how come that in this statement you didn't mention anywhere JNA members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I call them Chetniks too. It's not written anywhere, but I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But yesterday you even mentioned the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the police, and I even said that there was a Muslim among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand all that, sir. But just explain to me why you didn't say that on the 17th of June, 1992, only five or six days after those events? But it was only to the investigators that you said that. Just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will explain. I would like to ask you after such a trauma what you would have told if you would have experienced the disaster that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it may be helpful if we review a little bit more of that statement that's been put in, preferably in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say a few lines further on after hearing the man say "Let them suffer," speaking of the man who asked to be killed, you say: "I slowly pulled myself out from under the dead bodies." Did you find yourself under dead bodies as you've described in detail in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. That is where I found myself, because when they started shooting people in the back, people were turning around and falling. And this relative who held me by the hand was on top of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there are two passages I want your comment on that you haven't been asked about by the accused or Mr. Tapuskovic. You describe going off to the brush wood and waiting for night to fall, and then you say in this statement or it's recorded that you said: "From there I saw two more trucks loaded with people arrive and I heard machine fire." Did you in fact see the trucks arrive but only hear the machine-gun fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard the trucks very well when they arrived. True, on that day there were three trips. In the group I was in, there were 64 of us. Then they brought two more lots. And they opened fire at the same spot. I heard the fire, and I heard the trucks arriving. I wasn't far away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Did you actually see the trucks as this statement suggests or only hear them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it says I saw them. I just heard them coming to the same stop from which I had escaped the execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two lines further on where you calculated the number of people that would have been killed. You said this, and I'd like your comment on it: "I assumed that was done by the residents of Pilica." Why did you make that assumption and what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where it says that. I may have said about these 300 that stayed behind down there, that this may have been done by the locals of Pilica, by the inhabitants of Pilica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally on this topic, although one other question after it on the statement, a little bit further on after you deal with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people who'd been speaking of the murderers of the young man called Sane, you deal with, you're going to the house where the execution had taken place, and you say or your statement records you are saying that in the bushes, you saw them using forklift trucks to load the dead bodies onto the trucks, and you assume there were about 400. Did you actually see them loading bodies onto the trucks or did you deduce that that's what had been happening?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that the witness in his statement doesn't speak of a loader but of a bulldozer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters, Mr. Milosevic, don't know what a loader is and they used the word bulldozer, and I'm sure you know what a bulldozer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume you were giving your statement in your own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time, Witness B-1098. Mr. Nice, would you care to take over and straighten this out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What your statement, if you've got it there in front of you B-1098, appears to say at this passage is that you saw them using forklift trucks to load dead bodies into the trucks, and you assume that there were about 400. Now, when you were giving evidence yesterday you spoke of your deduction that there were bodies in the lorry with the tarpaulin around the side of it. Can you help us? Did you actually see loading of bodies onto the truck or did you simply deduce that in the way you suggested yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, when I was watching, it was a big truck with a -- like a container behind covered with a tarpaulin. And this same bulldozer was standing right next to the truck. The forklift would be loading the bodies. Then they would cover the struck with tarpaulin across the sides and thread it -- thread the rope through to tie it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this something you actually -- is this something you actually saw, that procedure, or is this something that you deduced, something that you inferred from what you did see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, this forklift, it was working all the time. And just then, people in civilian clothes were tying down the tarpaulin. So I thought that they were loading those bodies onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness certainly didn't give his statement in the English language. That is what I assume. And in the statement in the Serbian language on page 7, one but last paragraph it says, I'm reading the whole sentence up to the full stop: "I returned close to the house where the mass killing had taken place, and I saw a bulldozer loading bodies onto a truck," full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have the point. We have the point and the witness has explained. Let's move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question on the statement is at the foot of the page, Your Honour. It deals with a person who the witness did name in open session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-1098, you said this in your witness statement, during your stay in Medjedje, you heard that Vejsil Hamzic from Durokovci [phoen] had survived the execution because he had supposedly found himself in a group that was killed in the truck. He was still in Medjedje. Is that the process whereby you learned of this other survivor, although he was a survivor subsequently killed elsewhere in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I reached Zaseok, that is in free territory, I was told straight away by the inhabitants of Zaseok that another man had come from the execution. They had arrested him thinking he was someone else. Afterwards I found that Vejsil, but unfortunately he was killed during the war. I wish he were an alive and that he could testify because he survived the same as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the statement that you made just days after finding yourself in free territory, a statement you made in hospital, and you're giving an account there of how you learnt of Vejsil Hamzic. Is the account you give about learning about him a true one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I explained a moment ago that when I reached Zaseok on free territory, the people in Zaseok told me that another man had arrived and he was in the third group for the execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally these two or three questions. You heard me inform the Chamber this morning that you were interviewed in the hospital and that you'd been interviewed for television or something on a subsequent occasion at least once since. On those interviews, have you given the history of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's probable that I didn't say everything on television for my own safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you gave a general account of all these people being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew about these 400, but I said I didn't believe anybody had survived. And you have a recording, you can play it so that he should know what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has anybody until the accused started cross-examining you yesterday suggested to you that your account of these events is fabricated, fictional, made up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never has anyone done that prior to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally this, but answer it in general terms, please: To your knowledge, is the area where the people who you say were killed lived recently been re-populated by such of the people who lived there originally as have been able to return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area now, I think, is being re-populated. Not a hundred per cent, but I believe 90 per cent it has been re-populated .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has there been any suggestion in the course of that re-population that these hundreds of people, hundreds of men you described as having been killed at Karakaj are not dead at all and are actually in a position to come home and retake their properties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The women and children have come back and those who were killed will never come back to regain their property. They're done with. If I could now ask a question, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not of me because I've finished the questions I want to ask you, but if you ask the question of Their Honours, they may or may not indulge you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a few of these returnees of ours, Your Honours, went back there. As I said awhile ago, 90 per cent of the population has returned. And again, people are getting closer to each other, Serbs and Muslims. Any Serb you ask about these people, where they are and how they fared and where the graves are at least, they say, "How should we know? It's people from Yugoslavia who came." That's the kind of question or answer you'll get from any Serb who lives there. They say, "No way. We have no idea about this." And now he's telling me that the Yugoslav People's Army didn't take part in this. What about the Uzice Corps? What about all these other corps? That's what I can't understand. And now according to Milosevic, it's the witness who is making all of this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you want to exhibit these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think if I may respectfully say so, all the statements including the first statement that the accused was cross-examining on, the corrected statement that I think is included in the package you've got, it's about one page with the corrections on the interpretation, and the earlier statement made by the witness should probably be before you given that he is the sole survivor of these events and although there will be other evidence that will support it, I think insofar as it touches on movement of people to and from Karakaj and thereabouts and insofar as indeed it's supported by the evidence of the movements of the vehicle from Drinatrans, nevertheless, it is the material of the sole survivor and probably should be available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statements are those, first of all to the public or, rather, security services centre, Tuzla, 17th of June, 1992, to the Office of the Prosecutor, 24th of November, 1996, and a third statement is the corrected statement is the 9th of July, 2002. It might be convenient if all three of exhibited together.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 457.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we will make arrangements if possible to retain the witness here until tomorrow. We will provide copies of the two interviews today. I can't say that we'll be able to have transcripts of what is on those videos by tomorrow, but we'll do whatever we can to provide a written summary of what they contain, and perhaps we can deal tomorrow morning with the release of the witness finally from court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1098, for the moment that concludes your evidence. There has been, as you know, this material which has been found, this interview, and it may be that there are one or two questions that you may have to be asked about that. So if you can, we're going to ask you to remain here to deal with it, and you can talk to the Prosecution if there's anything relevant about it. But subject to that, you are free to go, and thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this additional examination, there is one thing that is quite unclear, Mr. May. There is one question that is totally unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't ask the witness any questions, he's finished giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not answering any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now what is the point you're making.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it. I want to say that Mr. Nice asked the witness to explain to him what he wrote in his statement. I assume that this was done by the villagers from Pilica. That's what it says in the statement. And if the witness said in response that this probably pertains to those 300 rather than to what he had testified about, which is not correct. So could you please be so kind as to take the translation. The translation is a good one. On page 3 of this statement that you looked at just now, just like I did, on page 3 of the English statement you will see that it is not correct, that the explanation refers to those 300 in Pilica. Somewhere around the middle of this big paragraph, in English, you have under quotation marks "Let them suffer." It will be quite obvious. You can see it on the left-hand margin. "Let them suffer." It's about after the second-third of that paragraph. And then the text: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... which Chetniks had left. And so that there was nobody around, I slowly pulled myself out from under the dead bodies, left the building and hid close by in some --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can read this. You cannot take up more time with these arguments. We have seen -- we have seen -- wait a moment. These documents have been exhibited and you can address us on it in due course, but we cannot waste more time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next witness, please. No, Mr. Milosevic, we have the point. We can read it. It's all in front of us, and now is not the time to make it. Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, are you calling the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think the usher is already on her way. Your Honour, the next witness is the Witness C-047, and he is also a protected witness with image -- pseudonym and image alteration.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness also has voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a request. I think it would be all right if this screen could be moved just a little bit. I cannot see the witnesses when I examine them, and I think it really wouldn't matter if the screen would be pulled just about 20 metres to the other side, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could see about that during the adjournment. We'll see what can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, could we briefly go into private session for some particulars related to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Witness C-047, during this adjournment and any others there may be, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to draw your attention to one particular fact so that that is clear. While the previous witness testified, I heard through the headsets, it probably came from the technical booth where they were looking through their interviews, but I was able to hear all the particulars, names, surname, and all these other particulars, but I assume that this was in closed -- in private session. But my associate who sits outside in the public gallery heard this interference, which means that his name was in fact disclosed. So I should like you to bear that in mind. I don't want there to be any mystifications as to who disclosed his name. You could hear it quite clearly. I also heard it through my headsets in the background. However, I did believe it was in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've had a report that the name did get out that way, and steps are being taken to ensure it doesn't happen again, and there will be suitable redactions, of course, in the transcript, and I'm sure the press won't report it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you meet Vojislav Seselj in the last part of 1990 in a gathering in a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. I met Vojislav Seselj in 1990 in a place called Mali Stapar in a restaurant there owned by Aleksandar Nikolic. He was the proprietor there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you attend this gathering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: From my friends in Civac, I heard this was somebody who was a royalist, who favoured the monarchy, who was opposed to communism and that he was coming to Mali Stapar to gather around him some people. We all knew that there would be a war, but as I said, he was an advocate of the monarchy. He was a Royalist at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Seselj on this gathering speak about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Seselj said there would be a war and that he was in favour of a monarchy, that an army should established, that we should fight communism and topple communism in Yugoslavia, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he refer to Croatia and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that there was unrest in Croatia and that the Croats were exerting pressure on the Serbs in a number of ways, through killings and in other ways, and that there would be a war and that the army, his army, Seselj's army or, rather, the Chetniks already had units that part of Backa. It is actually Western Backa with Jovo Ostojic at their head and that those Chetniks were being trained close to that locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you have information of what was actually going on in Croatia and how the Serbs were treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. Via the media I was able to follow the situation there, and there were news reports all the time that the Serbs were -- that maximum pressure had been exerted against the Serbs, that atrocities were being committed, that they were threatened. In a word, that they were in jeopardy, generally speaking, from the Croats, endangered from the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that gathering, did Seselj ask you to do something? Not you personally, but the people present to do something in your region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed it, and he said that in Subotica there were two men who were organising the Serbian Radical Party or, rather, collecting up a membership for the party from the North Backa district. And the goal of that rallying was to set up the Serbian Radical Party in those regions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Seselj was a royalist and was actually very much arguing against communism. Did you share these views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: That's how he introduced himself and presented himself as being. He showed a different side to him later on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the latter half of what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am a royalist myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last half sentence that you said. Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: I am also an advocate of royalism. I am for the monarchy. I am for the King.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period that followed, did you actually observe Seselj being -- opposing communism and parties related to communism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. At that time he did do so via the media. And of course at these meetings and rallies he always spoke out against communism, saying that it should be overthrown, put a stop to, and if necessary, this should be done through force of arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that came, was the SRS party, the Serbian Radical Party, actually fighting the SPS policy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: For a time, yes, it did, but later on he joined the politics and policies of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is "later on"? Which period do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: That means straight away in 1991. Towards the end of 1991, I realised that he was not in fact a royalist and that everything that he was doing he was in fact doing under the commands of the state in cohorts with the state and in agreement with the JNA and the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any difference in what Seselj said publicly and what he actually did when it comes to communism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed a maximum amount of differences. He would say one thing and do something quite different. He joined the communists and socialists, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he oppose the Serbian government, the policy of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Not after 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Seselj suggested to form a branch of the SRS party in the region. Did this indeed happen, and did you join that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Subotica, which is where I resided. I came into contact with Bozidar Vujic and Milan Stojanovic who had already established the Serbian Radical Party for the North Backa district with its centre and headquarters in Subotica, and I joined the two of them in organising the party, rallying members for the party. And at the same time, the Serbian Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that in that first gathering that Seselj mentioned a person Jovo Ostojic. What did he say about him and who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: He mention that had there was a man called Jovo Ostojic who was a great patriot, a Serb, who was rallying volunteers from the area of Western Backa, that he was training them and preparing them for war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the same thing -- was the same thing then also organised in Subotica, without going into details, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These volunteer forces that Jovo Ostojic established and that also were established in Subotica, are they usually referred to as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly what is a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Well, during the Second World War, the King's officers who were opposed to communism were called Chetniks, and they were led by a general named General Draza Mihajlovic. So for the most part, they were people who were monarchist, who were in favour of the King, who supported the King. And this tradition has persevered. It had to work illegally, underground, the Serbian Chetnik movement until 1990 or 1991, when Vojislav Seselj created the Serbian Chetnik movement within the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to their appearance, how can they are distinguished or could they be distinguished from other armed formation -- formations? Is there a special sign in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: They were people, men who were Serb oriented. They did not have any uniforms. They were not people who had graduated from regular army training or military -- had military experience and training. Usually Chetniks wore beards and the cockades which was a national emblem with the two-headed eagle and crown, and also they had a skull with the two bones Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which was the Chetnik emblem, insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a difference in appearance between the SRS Chetniks and the so-called White Eagles of Mirko Jovic? Could they also be distinguished from each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they could be distinguished by virtue of the insignia and symbols they wore and by virtue of their appearance I would say too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What was different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: The difference is that the White Eagles, as the name says, had the white eagle insignia. The Chetniks had the skull and bone insignia, the bones being crossed. So that was their symbol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you now a few documents related to the SRS party and the SCP, the Serbian Chetnik movement. The first one is tab 2. We have it also on Sanction. Just have a brief look at it and tell us whether you are familiar with the document called "Manifesto of the Serbian Radical Party for 1991."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this. I had it in my hands and I am familiar with the contents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to briefly address a few points in this manifesto, and in the introduction on the first page there is a reference to the founding Assembly in Kragujevac on the 23rd of February, 1991. Are you familiar with the fact that it was established officially then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1 you find a reference to -- that, "This party has in mind the restoration of the free, independent, and democratic Serbian state in the Balkans which will include the whole of Serbdom, all the Serbian lands, which means that within its frontiers will be, besides the current, imposed federal unit of Serbia itself, Serbian Macedonia, Serbian Montenegro, Serbian Bosnia, Serbian Herzegovina, Serbian Dubrovnik, Serbian Dalmatia, Serbian Lika, Serbian Kordun, Serbian Banja, Serbian Slavonia, and Serbian Baranja." Were you aware of that territorial claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one other fact I want to refer you to, and that's actually paragraph 25. Would you please go forward to paragraph 25. Paragraph 25 deals with Kosovo and Metohija and actually lists a lot of measures referring to the Kosovo Albanian population and including to expel 360.000 immigrants from Albania and their descendants related to that any state financial subsidy to the ethnic Albanian minorities be prevented. You see that the Albanians are addressed as Siptars. Was Kosovo an issue at that time for you and for the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this. I was in Kosovo on a number of occasions as a police officer and I saw what was going on there, the repressive measures against the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is at the last page of this document there is a reference to the support that the SRS supports the political efforts of the Serbian Democratic Party in the area of the current Croatia and the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina inter alia. These are the SDS parties in these countries, in these regions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document I would like to have you look at is the statute of Serbian Radical Party, and it's a document which has attached to it on the last page a decree, a decree of the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Justice referring that it is entered in the register political organisation in Serbia. Were you aware that it was registered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you please now look at the statute of the Serbian Radical Party, the newer one from, as it says on the last page, 1994. Are you also familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like you to briefly look at the Articles 1, 2, and 3. They all deal with the fight for the state unity and the struggle for unification of all Serbian lands, and there as also a reference to Serbian ethnic areas. Were you aware that this was one of the goals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would only now in relation to this statute refer you to paragraph 79 -- Article 79. If you please look at Article 79. There is a reference to collective members of the party, and it says here: "Collective members of the party are the Serbian Chetnik movement," and then something else follows. Does this mean that the members of the Serbian Chetnik movement were automatically also SRS members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: The members of the Serbian Chetnik movement had to be members of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Article 81, it says that the Serbian Chetnik movement, as a collective member, rallies its members for the following purposes, and then four of the purposes listed, basically organising, volunteers, organise assistance for fighters and the like. Is that what the Serbian Chetnik movement actually did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. That was the basic task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Article 82, you see here the reference to the highest organ of the SGP. It's the council of vojvoda consisting of all the vojvodas headed by the one who held the rank the longest. Could you say who that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. That was Vojislav Seselj who gained the title of vojvoda from the Chetnik vojvoda during the war, Vojvoda Djujic, Momcilo Djujic. And he was the oldest one in the movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is a vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: It is the highest title in the Serbian Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Article 85, you have actually listed who the conditions for a vojvoda. It says here the rank of vojvoda may be awarded to a person who fulfils all the following conditions, and there are the conditions. Does that mean a vojvoda usually is a fighter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: It doesn't have to mean that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I wonder if we could get the literal meaning of vojvoda in Serbia through help with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Vojvoda means "duke," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Duke. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here rank of vojvoda may be awarded to a person who fulfils all the following conditions it says distinguished fighter the next line also says distinguished fighter and the fourth condition is participant in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that is not necessarily a vojvoda. Who else could get such a position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Somebody who worked to organise the Serbian Chetnik movement. For example, in Northern Backa, rallying aid and assistance to Krajina, Slavonia, and Baranja. Somebody who had set up the military section of the Serbian radical movement, rallying supporters, sympathisers or fighters, volunteers, train them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to put to you the diagram, tab 4. It's the structure of the SRS in Vojvodina. This chart, was it actually prepared by the Prosecutor -- Prosecutor's office with your assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have Vojislav Seselj on the top of it and there is also the Main Board. Did it include Main Board members from other regions outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have highlighted here also a person, Jovan Glamocanin. He had a special function. What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Mr. Jovan Glamocanin was the coordinator. That is to say he helped set up the district boards, local boards of the Serbian Radical Party. He gave instructions, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the structures below this central level in Belgrade, we have it here for Vojvodina and Subotica. Would such a similar structure be established in other regions as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That should be enough. I would like now to go to tab 5, which is a policy platform of the Serbian Chetnik movement. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the English we cannot actually see from which time period it is, but in the Serbian first page could you see at what time this platform was actually published?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: I can't see that, but as far as I know, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously the witness was not given the first page. We could perhaps put it on the ELMO or just show it to the witness. I think we have to put it on the ELMO because Their Honours do not have it. Can we put the first page on the ELMO? From the first page, can you see a date? It's a little bit difficult to see, but can you see -- or when you look at the original, do you see a date there in the Cyrillic language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. That is July 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the emblem, what is that? What emblem is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: It is the emblem of the Serbian Radical Party, Greater Serbia, the journal that was published by the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough for the ELMO, but I would like to address a few points in the platform. In paragraph one of the platform we have the restoration of a free independent democratic Serbian state in the Balkans, and we have also the reference to the various regions that belong to this state. And is that the same as in the SRS programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I would like to refer you to paragraph 11. There is a reference to World War II genocide. And after this reference to the world war genocide -- World War II genocide, it then also says: "To do so requires a detailed and comprehensive registration of the victims and identification of the perpetrators of the crimes, particularly taking into account the restoration of the independent State of Croatia and the appearance of the new Ustasha leaders as well as the general protection of the Serbian population who are presently endangered by the new genocidal policy." Was that the point of view the Serbian Chetnik movement and the SRS party, that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also would like to refer you to paragraph 20 where we again have also the special methods and measures in relation to Kosovo and Metohija. You're familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just another document, statute of the Serbian Chetnik movement. I just would like you to have a look at it briefly and tell us whether you are aware and familiar with this statute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That should be enough. And I would like to go briefly into private session, Your Honour, because we have to review a -- a chart with a name on it. It's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more document in relation to a structure that we saw in the last diagram. In the last diagram, we saw the war -- the War Staff, and here is a document, minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting of the 1st October, 1991, Crisis Staff meeting of the Serbian Radical Party, and we see here the name from Crisis Staff is changed to War Staff, as you mentioned before. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And now I would take you to some insignia?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it would be Exhibit 349, tab 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where we have two -- we have actually the first insignia on the screen. What is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-047
utterances.text: Yes. It is the patch of the Serbian Chetnik movement, the emblem or insignia that is worn on the left sleeve of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have a flag of that kind?
